steps.body: When a factor repeats, its zero has **multiplicity**: in f(x) = (x + 2)(x − 1)², the zero 1 has multiplicity 2 and −2 has multiplicity 1. The graph tells them apart: at an **odd** multiplicity it **crosses** the axis; at an **even** one it **bounces** — touching without passing through.

widget.prompt: p(x) = (x + 2)(x − 1)²(x − 3). Set the sign of p on each interval — the sketch will follow your claim.
widget.successFeedback: + − − +. The sign flips at −2 and at 3, but NOT at 1: the double root touches zero and comes straight back the way it came. Odd crosses, even bounces — and you produced that rule instead of being handed it.
widget.crossFeedback: A single root is a crossing: the curve goes through zero and out the other side, so the sign MUST flip there. Look either side of −2 and of 3.
widget.bounceFeedback: You flipped the sign across x = 1 — but that root is DOUBLE. The curve reaches zero and turns back, leaving on the side it arrived from. An even root never changes the sign.

predict.prompt: At the double root x = 1, the graph of p(x) = (x + 2)(x − 1)²(x − 3)…

options.label: Bounces — touches the axis and turns back

predict.reveal: An even power can't change sign: (x − 1)² is positive on BOTH sides of 1, so p kisses the axis there and turns back. The odd roots at −2 and 3 cross; even multiplicity bounces.

cml.actionGoal: Build interval signs and use multiplicity to make every intercept cross or bounce consistently with the factorization.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Change the double root to multiplicity 3 without moving it. Which interval sign must change, and how must the graph behave at that intercept?

explanation.prompt: Why does an even-multiplicity root bounce while an odd-multiplicity root crosses?

options.label: An even power has the same sign on both sides of zero, while an odd power changes sign.
options.feedback: Exactly — multiplicity controls whether the factor changes the product’s sign.

options.label: Even roots are always higher on the graph than odd roots.
options.feedback: Both root types have output zero; the distinction is the sign on either side.

steps.body: Why the bounce: near x = 1, (x − 1)² is a tiny **square** — never negative — so the factor can't drag f across the axis; f grazes it and turns back. An odd power does change sign, so the graph pushes through. Sign change ⟺ crossing.

explanationVariants: (x + 1)³ has odd multiplicity 3: the graph crosses at −1 (flattening as it goes).
Odd powers change sign across their zero, so the curve passes through.

widget.prompt: In f(x) = (x + 1)³(x − 2)², what does the graph do at x = −1?

options.label: crosses the axis (flattened)
options.feedback: Right — multiplicity 3 is odd: through it goes, with a flat kiss.

options.label: bounces off the axis
options.feedback: Bouncing needs an EVEN multiplicity — 3 is odd, so it crosses.

options.label: has a hole there
options.feedback: Polynomials never have holes — every zero is a touch or a crossing.

options.label: jumps over it
options.feedback: Polynomial graphs are unbroken — at a zero they either cross or bounce; here, cross.

steps.body: Make both multiplicities control the graph.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = (x + 1)³(x − 2)², set each interval sign and make the graph show what happens at both zeros.
widget.successFeedback: The sign flips at x = −1 and stays the same at x = 2. The cubic factor crosses; the squared factor bounces.
widget.crossFeedback: Multiplicity 3 is odd, so the sign must change at x = −1.
widget.bounceFeedback: Multiplicity 2 is even, so the sign must stay the same across x = 2.

explanationVariants: Expanding (x + 1)³(x − 2)² would give a leading x⁵.

widget.prompt: What is the degree of f(x) = (x + 1)³(x − 2)²?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 is only the count of DISTINCT zeros — the degree adds the exponents: 3 + 2 = 5.
Exponents ADD across multiplied factors (3 + 2), they don't multiply: degree 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 3 + 2 = 5 — the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra's bookkeeping: 5 zeros counting repeats.

explanationVariants: Degree 4, but only two DISTINCT zeros (5 and −5): two intercepts, one crossing spot each... both squared, so both bounces.
Multiplicities eat intercepts: (x − 5)²(x + 5)² meets the axis at just 5 and −5.

widget.prompt: How many DISTINCT x-intercepts does f(x) = (x − 5)²(x + 5)² have?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the degree (2 + 2) — the graph touches the axis at only the 2 distinct zeros, 5 and −5.
Both factors do reach zero — at x = 5 and x = −5 the graph bounces on the axis.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two distinct zeros, 5 and −5 (each a bounce): 2 intercepts.

explanationVariants: x² bounces at 0 (even), (x − 4) crosses at 4 (odd): bounce then cross.
Check each exponent's parity: 2 at the origin, 1 at four.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = x²(x − 4), what does the graph do at its zeros?

options.label: bounces at 0, crosses at 4
options.feedback: Right — even multiplicity 2 at the origin, odd 1 at four.

options.label: crosses at 0, bounces at 4
options.feedback: The parities are the other way: the SQUARE (even) bounces, the single factor crosses.

options.label: crosses at both
options.feedback: x² can't change sign, so the graph can't cross at 0 — it bounces there.

options.label: bounces at both
options.feedback: (x − 4) has odd multiplicity 1 — the graph passes straight through at 4.

hints: Find each zero's multiplicity: the exponent on its factor.
x² gives multiplicity 2 at x = 0; (x − 4) gives 1 at x = 4.

steps.body: The exponent on a factor decides: even bounces, odd crosses.
takeaways: Even multiplicity: the graph touches and turns back; odd: it passes through.
Degree = sum of all multiplicities — every polynomial of degree n has n zeros counting repeats.
steps.teaser: Next: two theorems that find factors by plugging in a single number.

concept.body: Even exponent → bounce; odd exponent → cross. In (x − 6)², the exponent at the zero 6 is 2.

explanationVariants: Multiplicity 2 is even: the graph bounces at 6.
A squared factor never goes negative, so it can't carry the graph across.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = (x − 6)², what does the graph do at x = 6?

options.label: bounces off the axis
options.feedback: Right — even multiplicity: touch and turn.

options.label: crosses the axis
options.feedback: A square never changes sign, so the graph can't get through — it bounces.

options.label: skips x = 6
options.feedback: (x − 6)² IS zero at 6 — the graph touches the axis right there.

options.label: breaks into two pieces
options.feedback: Polynomial graphs are one unbroken curve — at 6 this one just kisses the axis.
